messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elena Weiss was 58 when she came for treatment, a long-serving city council member known in her district for staying composed through budget fights, angry public comment, and late-night committee sessions. Years earlier, before entering local politics, she had spent several months as a relief worker in a war zone. What stayed with her was not a single coherent story but a set of stark images from one afternoon at a field clinic after shelling nearby. She remembered crouching beside a concrete wall, the air powdered with dust, hearing a man somewhere close by dragging in harsh, heavy breaths. Then there was another blast, loud enough to shake the room and send debris across the floor. In her mind the event existed mostly as flashes: a bloodied sleeve, a child’s shoe near an overturned cot, light cutting through smoke. Even when she described it now, she said it felt strangely as if it had happened to somebody else, as though she were reporting scenes she had seen rather than something she had lived through herself.

In the months after she came home, those fragments began forcing themselves into her mind without warning. The memories did not arrive as a narrative she could place in the past; they came as pictures, abrupt and uninvited, and the sense of distance from them only made them more unsettling. Because they felt alien and outside her control, Elena had come to believe there was something permanently altered in her. What frightened her most was the idea that she would never feel normal emotions again, that whatever part of her used to respond warmly or freely had been blunted in that clinic and left there.

She also grew convinced that thinking directly about the war-zone experience would be more than upsetting; it would overwhelm her completely. She had become certain that if she let herself dwell on those scenes, she would not be able to handle what followed. That belief shaped the way the memories lived in her mind: the more she tried to push them away, the more they seemed to break through on their own terms, as disconnected images and sudden mental intrusions that she could neither soften nor fully understand. Their involuntary quality reinforced her sense that the world was dangerous and that her own mind was no longer reliably under her control.

Her triggers were woven into daily life in ways that made this feel inescapable. At city hall, if a microphone boomed unexpectedly during a council meeting or a construction bang sounded from the street below, she would instantly hear the remembered explosion again, and the old visual fragments would force their way back. Sometimes it was quieter and more intimate: in a crowded hallway after session, catching the sound of someone breathing heavily after climbing the stairs could bring up the image of that injured man in the clinic before she even knew what had set her off. In those moments, the trigger did not remain just a sound in the present. It opened directly onto the alien, picture-like memory, and once the memory was there she felt again that the world was fundamentally unsafe.

That conclusion had begun to alter what she noticed around her. Because she believed danger was everywhere, Elena listened for sharp bangs and found herself tensing at any strained or labored breathing in public spaces. In council chambers she scanned the room when staff shifted equipment, and during neighborhood events she tracked noises from traffic, generators, or construction with a vigilance she could not shut off. Her expectation of threat made these sounds stand out quickly, and once noticed they were harder to dismiss, as if her own fear had trained her attention toward the very cues most likely to set everything off again.

The memories themselves also made the triggers more potent. After a morning intrusion, she could spend the rest of the day acutely sensitive to every abrupt sound, primed for another explosion that she knew rationally was not coming. The image of dust and shattered space lingered just close enough that a slammed door at city hall or heavy breathing from someone speaking angrily at the podium seemed to belong to the same world as the clinic. Each recurrence confirmed her belief that normal feeling had drained out of her life; she described herself as going through the motions with constituents and colleagues, present in body but emotionally flat.

What finally brought Elena to seek help was not one dramatic collapse but the tightening sense that her life had narrowed around these moments. She could still perform her duties, but public meetings had become ordeals organized around anticipation of noise, and she dreaded the involuntary images that followed her home afterward. She came in afraid that if she ever stopped holding the memories at arm’s length, they would swallow her; she also came with a quieter hope that they might someday feel like her own past instead of an ongoing threat, and that she might recover some sense of ordinary feeling before the rest of her life was lived in permanent alarm.
